6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, each serving a distinct role.

12	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 52\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary where model capability is insufficient.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP gains are associated with strong LP-quality alignment (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two factors constrain selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) limits the available headroom, and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample) prevents exploiting the remainder.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 48.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation disentangles the two factors: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5--0.7; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Within fixed settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness: the SciERC epoch ablation shows LP gains varying with training-induced degeneracy (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}). Across 23 dataset-model-temperature configurations ($N{=}8$), however, degeneracy alone does not predict LP direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$); LP signal quality and dataset characteristics are required for cross-dataset prediction.
Temperature and training convergence are controllable levers for degeneracy (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 86.5\% vs.\ Qwen 48.4\% on CoNLL; LLaMA 23.4\% vs.\ Qwen 12.7\% on Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Our diagnostic motivates a shift from instance-level selection to entity-level construction (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS; Appendix~\ref{app:dals}) and MBR selection both fail to reliably beat greedy; degeneracy-gated selection (DGS) shows mixed results (Few-NERD $+0.92$~pp, SciERC $+0.71$~pp non-significant, CoNLL sign-reversal across models; Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms: it aggregates across samples rather than ranking them, recovering $+1.67$\,pp (SciERC) and $+0.88$\,pp (Few-NERD) via LP-weighted entity aggregation (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}).
Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), and a simple alignment-based gating protocol selects the better method per dataset.
For practitioners, QE-based selective prediction provides an orthogonal, immediate payoff: routing low-confidence instances to human review yields $+5$--$8$\,pp at 80\% coverage without requiring multi-sample generation at inference time.

Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding. Selection headroom may re-emerge in settings with greater output diversity: in-context learning without fine-tuning, ensemble/mixture-of-experts architectures, or models with systematic overconfidence. Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable can still use structural signals for quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45).

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Two factors shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples produce identical F1, (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) limits the available headroom; (b)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to MBR utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably predict instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.38 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82, CoNLL EM). \textbf{Right}: quality estimation does not translate to selection; all methods approximately match greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (AUPRC 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
    LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as the correct self-consistency analogy.}
    Rather than selecting one of $N$ outputs, LP-weighted entity aggregation yields $+1.67$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$) and $+0.88$\,pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes all three evaluated datasets.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Supervised Signal Combination}\label{app:supervised_combination}

Supervised classifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) trained on all five signals (5-fold CV, 3-seed mean, SciERC, $N{=}16$, $+17.9$~pp headroom) all perform at or below greedy (F1${=}0.644$; LR: $-0.4$~pp; MLP: $-1.6$~pp; RF: $-3.1$~pp).
Adding pairwise interaction features does not help (AUROC 0.634 vs.\ 0.638).
To test whether richer representations could close the gap, we train a DeBERTa-v3-base verifier that encodes input-output pairs and predicts per-sample F1.
DeBERTa achieves $\rho{=}0.329{\pm}0.087$ (5-fold CV, 3 seeds). Despite moderate quality prediction, selection utility is poor: on SciERC, DeBERTa closes $-26.5{\pm}26.5$\% of the oracle gap (13 of 15 runs negative; vs.\ LP's $+4.2{\pm}10.7$\%); on Few-NERD, DeBERTa recovers only $+3.5$\% (single 80/20 split; vs.\ LP's $+16.3$\%).
Cross-dataset transfer fails entirely ($-27$\% to $-72$\% gap closure).
Neither handcrafted signal combinations nor learned text representations close the selection gap; only model-internal log-probability provides meaningful selection signal, consistent with an information asymmetry between the generating model and external observers.

\section{Hidden State Probes}\label{app:hidden_probe}

The preceding negative results in the main text (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) suggest the bottleneck is model-internal rather than a feature engineering problem.
We test this directly by training probes on the generating model's hidden representations.

\paragraph{Setup.}
For each of $N{=}8$ samples per instance, we extract the mean-pooled final-layer hidden state ($d{=}4096$) from the generating Qwen3-8B model and train a linear probe and a two-layer MLP (hidden dim${=}256$) to predict per-sample F1 (5-fold CV, 3 seeds).

\centering
\small
\caption{Hidden state probes vs.\ LP for sample selection (5-fold CV ${\times}$ 3 seeds). $\rho$: Spearman correlation with per-sample F1. Sel.\ F1: selection F1. Gap\%: oracle gap closure. SciERC greedy${=}0.644$, oracle${=}0.775$.}
\label{tab:hidden_probe}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l ccc cc@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{SciERC}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Few-NERD}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6}
Method & $\rho$ & Sel.\ F1 & Gap\% & $\rho$ & Gap\% \\
\midrule
LP & .283 & $\mathbf{.650}$ & $+$4.8 & .606 & 12.3 \\
Hidden Linear & $.179{\pm}.019$ & $.613{\pm}.002$ & $-$23.4 & \multicolumn{2}{c}{---} \\
Hidden MLP & $\mathbf{.388{\pm}.013}$ & $.637{\pm}.003$ & $-$5.1 & $\mathbf{.629{\pm}.007}$ & 11.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Cross-dataset asymmetry.}
On SciERC, the MLP probe achieves higher quality correlation than LP ($\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ $0.283$, $+37$\%); hidden states encode information beyond what LP captures.
Yet higher correlation does not yield better selection: MLP selection F1 ($0.637$) falls below LP's ($0.650$), with gap closure turning negative ($-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; Table~\ref{tab:hidden_probe}).
The linear probe performs worse still ($\rho{=}0.179$, gap closure $-23.4$\%).
On Few-NERD, the MLP provides no increment over LP (gap closure $11.7$\% vs.\ $12.3$\%).
A learned token-level LP aggregator (1D CNN over per-token log-probabilities) matches mean LP on Few-NERD (gap closure $56.4$\% vs.\ $55.8$\%); LP's bottleneck is not token aggregation.
The correlation-selection gap extends to model-internal representations: in the high-capability regime (greedy F1${=}0.644$), inter-sample F1 differences are small enough that improved ranking provides no marginal selection value, consistent with the capability-diversity tension (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Multi-Seed Stability}\label{app:multiseed}

Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} reports quality estimation metrics across three random seeds for both model families on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Two factors shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples produce identical F1, (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) limits the available headroom; (b)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to MBR utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably predict instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.39 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82, CoNLL EM). \textbf{Right}: quality estimation does not translate to instance-level selection; all methods approximately match greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. Entity-level construction bypasses this gap (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (AUPRC 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
    LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as the correct self-consistency analogy.}
    Rather than selecting one of $N$ outputs, LP-weighted entity aggregation yields $+1.67$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$) and $+0.88$\,pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes all three evaluated datasets.
\end{enumerate}

3	\paragraph{Implications.}

17	Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).
18	
19	\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
20	QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP gains are associated with strong LP-quality alignment (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 48.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation disentangles the two factors: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5--0.7; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Within fixed settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness: the SciERC epoch ablation shows LP gains varying with training-induced degeneracy (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}). Across 23 dataset-model-temperature configurations ($N{=}8$), however, degeneracy alone does not predict LP direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$); LP signal quality and dataset characteristics are required for cross-dataset prediction.
Temperature and training convergence are controllable levers for degeneracy (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 86.5\% vs.\ Qwen 48.4\% on CoNLL; LLaMA 23.4\% vs.\ Qwen 12.7\% on Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Our diagnostic motivates a shift from instance-level selection to entity-level construction (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS; Appendix~\ref{app:dals}) and MBR selection both fail to reliably beat greedy; degeneracy-gated selection (DGS) shows mixed results (Few-NERD $+0.92$~pp, SciERC $+0.71$~pp non-significant, CoNLL sign-reversal across models; Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).

Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), and a simple alignment-based gating protocol selects the better method per dataset.
For practitioners, QE-based selective prediction provides an orthogonal, immediate payoff: routing low-confidence instances to human review yields $+5$--$8$\,pp at 80\% coverage without requiring multi-sample generation at inference time.

\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}
Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding. Selection headroom may re-emerge in settings with greater output diversity: in-context learning without fine-tuning, ensemble/mixture-of-experts architectures, or models with systematic overconfidence. Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable can still use structural signals for quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45).

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where LP-quality alignment is strong, but gains are absent elsewhere despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We diagnose two causes: instance degeneracy (13\textendash 87\%) and weak LP-quality alignment; degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations).
The correct self-consistency analogy for structured outputs is entity-level \textit{construction}: aggregating entities across samples improves F1 by $+0.88$ to $+1.67$\,pp ($p{<}0.005$) on datasets where instance-level selection fails or is marginal. Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment; an alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes all three evaluated datasets.
\end{abstract}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP gains are associated with strong LP-quality alignment (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two factors constrain selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) limits the available headroom, and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample) prevents exploiting the remainder.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 48.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp: per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation disentangles the two factors: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5--0.7; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Within fixed settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness: the SciERC epoch ablation shows LP gains varying with training-induced degeneracy (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}). Across 23 dataset-model-temperature configurations ($N{=}8$), however, degeneracy alone does not predict LP direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$); LP signal quality and dataset characteristics are required for cross-dataset prediction.
Temperature and training convergence are controllable levers for degeneracy (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 86.5\% vs.\ Qwen 48.4\% on CoNLL; LLaMA 23.4\% vs.\ Qwen 12.7\% on Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Our diagnostic motivates a shift from instance-level selection to entity-level construction (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS; Appendix~\ref{app:dals}) and MBR selection both fail to reliably beat greedy; degeneracy-gated selection (DGS) shows mixed results (Few-NERD $+0.92$~pp, SciERC $+0.71$~pp non-significant, CoNLL sign-reversal across models; Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms: it aggregates across samples rather than ranking them, recovering $+1.67$\,pp (SciERC) and $+0.88$\,pp (Few-NERD) via LP-weighted entity aggregation (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}).
Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}), and a simple alignment-based gating protocol selects the better method per dataset.
For practitioners, QE-based selective prediction provides an orthogonal, immediate payoff: routing low-confidence instances to human review yields $+5$--$8$\,pp at 80\% coverage without requiring multi-sample generation at inference time.

\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}
Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding. Selection headroom may re-emerge in settings with greater output diversity: in-context learning without fine-tuning, ensemble/mixture-of-experts architectures, or models with systematic overconfidence. Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable can still use structural signals for quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45).
